newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia space flight control tense watching Mir.
newsitem.headline: Russia space flight control tense watching Mir.

text.p: For a brief moment on Thursday the flight director, a veteran cosmonaut himself, lost patience with the crew of the crippled Russian space station fighting for survival after a setback in its power system.

"This is a kindergarten," a frustrated Vladimir Solovyov said aloud at Mission Control outside Moscow after ending a conversation with the crew of the Mir station, who had plunged into a new crisis by mistakenly unplugging a vital computer.
"Have you switched off everything?" he shouted during a radio linkup as cosmonauts sat in the Mir's escape capsule. "Switch off everything on the left side!"
Mission Control buzzed with nervous energy as experts crowded around various terminals in the central hall full of computers trying to figure out a solution to the latest challenge.
"There is a tension in a hall," said one engineer. "But there is no panic. We are under constant pressure with something new happening every day."

Yet five rows of monitors on the wall were blank throughout the day as the Mir, deprived of most of its energy after the incident, was unable to transmit video data. A slow and obsolete dot matrix printer chugging away on top of a free standing computer seemed to highlight the technology cutoff.

Outside the main Mission Control hall, Russian and NASA officials sat under a bust of Soviet leader Vladimir Lenin and a mosaic of the first man in space, Russia's Yuri Gagarin, as they examined detailed photos of the Mir interior.
"You're over-stressed and it would be good if you could remember 50 percent of what I say," one Russian told an American NASA official.
Tension in the Mission Control peaked as the orbiting crew came into radio contact every hour or so as they passed over radio relay stations on their two-hourly orbits of Earth.
"What alarm as that going off?" Solovyov asked the crew at one point.
A small crowd of engineers gathered at the side of the room to watch. Some spoke out with quick advice as they watched the seconds tick away to the end of the communications window.

On the surface many showed a cool confidence that the latest crisis could be overcome. But with the power off in the station's main module and the oxygen supply limited, the crew were clearly working against the clock to save the ship.
Officials said the pressure and temperature should be fine for two or three days more and the oxygen supply for five.
Mission Control officials said they had wethered similar crises before.

"The situation is no worse than it was when they turned of the orientation system after the crash on June 25," said deputy flight director, Viktor Blagov. "This is not the first occurence and we have always succeeded before."
